# Lesson 34 — Original Model Configurations: Base vs. Big Transformer

Today we’ll reconstruct the **exact model configurations used in the 2017 paper**, and use the numbers to understand what they actually mean architecturally.

**Source of truth:** the original _Attention Is All You Need_ paper.

## 1. Learning objective

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to look at:

> **Transformer Base**  
> `N=6, d_model=512, d_ff=2048, h=8`

and explain **what every number means, where it appears in the architecture, and how it changes the computation**.

We will also compare it with the **Big** configuration without treating “bigger” as merely “more layers.”

---

# 2. First: What are Base and Big?

The paper experimented with two principal Transformer configurations:

- **Base**
    
- **Big**
    

They use essentially the **same architecture**.

The important idea is:

> **Big Transformer is not a fundamentally different architecture. It is a larger parameterization of the same Transformer design.**

Think of it like the same blueprint built with larger rooms and more capacity.

---

# 3. The original configuration table

The paper reports the following configurations:

|Hyperparameter|Base|Big|
|---|---|---|
|Encoder layers|6|6|
|Decoder layers|6|6|
|dmodeld_{model}|512|1024|
|dffd_{ff}|2048|4096|
|Attention heads|8|16|
|dkd_k|64|64|
|dvd_v|64|64|
|Dropout|0.1|0.3|
|Parameters|~65M|~213M|

The striking thing is that **the number of encoder and decoder layers stays at 6**.

Instead, Big substantially increases the **width** of the representations and the number of attention heads.

---

# 4. Start from the architecture

Remember the basic Transformer:

```
                 INPUT
                   │
              Embedding
                   │
          Positional Encoding
                   │
          ┌────────▼────────┐
          │ Encoder × 6     │
          └────────┬────────┘
                   │
             Encoder output
                   │
                   ▼
Target → Embedding
                   │
          Positional Encoding
                   │
          ┌────────▼────────┐
          │ Decoder × 6     │
          └────────┬────────┘
                   │
              Linear layer
                   │
                Logits
                   │
               Softmax
                   │
          Vocabulary probs
```

The Base and Big models use this same high-level structure.

---

# 5. What does N=6N=6 mean?

The paper defines:

N=6N=6

for both encoder and decoder stacks.

That means:

```
Encoder:

Input
 ↓
Encoder Layer 1
 ↓
Encoder Layer 2
 ↓
Encoder Layer 3
 ↓
Encoder Layer 4
 ↓
Encoder Layer 5
 ↓
Encoder Layer 6
 ↓
Encoder output
```

And independently:

```
Decoder:

Target representation
 ↓
Decoder Layer 1
 ↓
Decoder Layer 2
 ↓
Decoder Layer 3
 ↓
Decoder Layer 4
 ↓
Decoder Layer 5
 ↓
Decoder Layer 6
 ↓
Decoder output
```

So:

N=6N=6

does **not** mean six total Transformer layers.

It means:

6 encoder layers+6 decoder layers6\text{ encoder layers}+6\text{ decoder layers}

for a total of **12 stacked layers**.

---

# 6. Why stack layers?

This connects directly to our earlier lessons.

One attention layer can perform:

> "Let each token gather information from other tokens."

But one transformation may not be enough.

Suppose:

```
The animal didn't cross the road because it was tired.
```

A layer can build contextual relationships.

A subsequent layer receives those already-contextualized representations and can perform another transformation.

Conceptually:

```
Raw token representation
        ↓
Layer 1
        ↓
contextual representation
        ↓
Layer 2
        ↓
more refined representation
        ↓
Layer 3
        ↓
...
        ↓
Layer 6
```

Each layer operates on the representations produced by the previous layer.

### Important distinction

This does **not** mean:

> Layer 1 = nouns  
> Layer 2 = verbs  
> Layer 3 = grammar

That would be an unsupported interpretation.

The paper does not assign such human-readable functions to individual layers.

---

# 7. dmodeld_{model}: the central width

This is one of the most important numbers.

For Base:

dmodel=512d_{model}=512

For Big:

dmodel=1024d_{model}=1024

This is the dimensionality of the representation carried through the Transformer.

Imagine:

```
Token
 ↓
Embedding
 ↓
512-dimensional vector       Base
```

or:

```
Token
 ↓
Embedding
 ↓
1024-dimensional vector      Big
```

So if:

B=2B=2

and sequence length:

T=10T=10

then Base embedding output is:

[2,10,512][2,10,512]

while Big produces:

[2,10,1024][2,10,1024]

---

# 8. Why is dmodeld_{model} so important?

Because it appears everywhere.

For example:

```
Embedding
    ↓
[B,T,d_model]
    ↓
Multi-head attention
    ↓
[B,T,d_model]
    ↓
FFN
    ↓
[B,T,d_model]
```

The Transformer repeatedly transforms representations while generally preserving this outer model dimension.

For Base:

512→512512\rightarrow512

For Big:

1024→10241024\rightarrow1024

through the major sublayers.

---

# 9. Multi-head attention

Now the numbers become interesting.

Base:

h=8h=8

Big:

h=16h=16

where hh is the number of attention heads.

Base therefore has:

```
512-dimensional model
        ↓
8 heads
        ↓
64 dimensions/head
```

because:

8×64=5128\times64=512

Big:

```
1024-dimensional model
        ↓
16 heads
        ↓
64 dimensions/head
```

because:

16×64=102416\times64=1024

This is an important design relationship in the original configurations.

---

# 10. dkd_k and dvd_v

Recall:

Q=XWQQ=XW^Q

K=XWKK=XW^K

V=XWVV=XW^V

For each head, the paper uses:

dk=64d_k=64

and

dv=64d_v=64

for the configurations in this table.

Therefore one Base head looks like:

```
X
[B,T,512]
   │
   ├── WQ → Q [B,T,64]
   ├── WK → K [B,T,64]
   └── WV → V [B,T,64]
```

After attention:

```
Head output
[B,T,64]
```

Eight heads give:

8×64=5128\times64=512

and therefore:

```
Concat
[B,T,512]
```

---

# 11. Big model shape

For Big:

dmodel=1024d_{model}=1024

and:

h=16h=16

with:

dk=dv=64d_k=d_v=64

So:

```
Input
[B,T,1024]
       │
       ├── Head 1 → [B,T,64]
       ├── Head 2 → [B,T,64]
       ├── ...
       └── Head 16 → [B,T,64]
```

Concatenate:

16×64=102416\times64=1024

giving:

[B,T,1024][B,T,1024]

This is an elegant way to increase attention capacity while keeping each individual head's dimension at 64.

---

# 12. Feed-forward dimension

Now look at:

dffd_{ff}

Base:

dff=2048d_{ff}=2048

Big:

dff=4096d_{ff}=4096

Recall the original FFN:

FFN(x)=max⁡(0,xW1+b1)W2+b2FFN(x) = \max(0,xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2

The dimensional flow is:

### Base

512→2048→512512\rightarrow2048\rightarrow512

### Big

1024→4096→10241024\rightarrow4096\rightarrow1024

Visualized:

```
BASE

512
 ↓
Linear
 ↓
2048
 ↓
ReLU
 ↓
512
```

and:

```
BIG

1024
 ↓
Linear
 ↓
4096
 ↓
ReLU
 ↓
1024
```

So the inner FFN dimension is **four times** dmodeld_{model}:

2048=4(512)2048=4(512)

and:

4096=4(1024)4096=4(1024)

---

# 13. Why make the FFN wider?

Remember the distinction:

### Attention

> Who should this token interact with?

### Feed-forward network

> After receiving contextual information, how should this representation be transformed?

Attention mixes information **between positions**.

The FFN transforms information **within each position**.

So increasing dffd_{ff} gives the per-token transformation more capacity.

---

# 14. Complete Base tensor flow

Let's make this concrete.

Suppose:

B=2B=2

T=10T=10

and:

dmodel=512d_{model}=512

Input token IDs:

[2,10][2,10]

Embedding:

[2,10,512][2,10,512]

After positional encoding:

[2,10,512][2,10,512]

### Q/K/V

Conceptually:

Q,K,V:[2,10,512]Q,K,V: [2,10,512]

Then split into eight heads:

[2,8,10,64][2,8,10,64]

So:

```
B = 2
h = 8
T = 10
dk = 64
```

Attention scores:

QKTQK^T

produce:

[2,8,10,10][2,8,10,10]

Why 10×1010\times10?

Because every token can compare itself against every token.

Then:

```
scores
[2,8,10,10]

      ↓ softmax

attention weights
[2,8,10,10]

      ↓ multiply V

head output
[2,8,10,64]
```

Concatenate heads:

[2,10,512][2,10,512]

Then output projection:

[2,10,512][2,10,512]

---

# 15. Big tensor flow

Now change:

dmodel=1024d_{model}=1024

and:

h=16h=16

For the same:

B=2,T=10B=2,\quad T=10

Embedding:

[2,10,1024][2,10,1024]

Split heads:

[2,16,10,64][2,16,10,64]

Attention scores:

[2,16,10,10][2,16,10,10]

Each head still has:

dk=64d_k=64

After attention:

[2,16,10,64][2,16,10,64]

Concatenate:

[2,10,1024][2,10,1024]

So the key difference is:

```
BASE                         BIG

[B,T,512]                    [B,T,1024]
     ↓                             ↓
8 × 64 heads                 16 × 64 heads
     ↓                             ↓
[B,8,T,64]                   [B,16,T,64]
     ↓                             ↓
concat                        concat
     ↓                             ↓
[B,T,512]                    [B,T,1024]
```

---

# 16. Parameter-count intuition

The larger model has substantially more parameters.

The paper reports approximately:

65 million65\text{ million}

for Base and:

213 million213\text{ million}

for Big.

But **why** does the count increase so much?

Let's inspect the major sources.

---

## 17. Attention projection parameters

For a simplified view, each attention block has learned projection matrices:

WQ,WK,WV,WOW^Q,\quad W^K,\quad W^V,\quad W^O

Each is related to dmodeld_{model}.

For Base, the combined projection sizes are approximately:

512×512512\times512

for each of the four major projections.

So roughly:

4(5122)4(512^2)

parameters, ignoring biases.

That's:

4(262,144)=1,048,5764(262,144) = 1,048,576

about **1.05 million** parameters per multi-head attention module.

---

# 18. Big attention parameters

For Big:

dmodel=1024d_{model}=1024

So approximately:

4(10242)4(1024^2)

=4(1,048,576)=4(1,048,576)

=4,194,304=4,194,304

about **4.2 million** parameters.

Notice something important:

1024=2(512)1024=2(512)

but:

10242=4(5122)1024^2=4(512^2)

So doubling the model width can approximately **quadruple** the size of these square projection matrices.

---

# 19. FFN parameter growth

The FFN is even more revealing.

Base:

512→2048→512512\rightarrow2048\rightarrow512

Ignoring biases:

512(2048)+2048(512)512(2048)+2048(512)

=2(512)(2048)=2(512)(2048)

=2,097,152=2,097,152

roughly **2.1M parameters per FFN**.

Big:

1024→4096→10241024\rightarrow4096\rightarrow1024

giving:

2(1024)(4096)2(1024)(4096)

=8,388,608=8,388,608

roughly **8.4M parameters**.

Again:

8.4M≈4×2.1M8.4M\approx4\times2.1M

So widening the model has a strong effect on parameter count.

---

# 20. Important research insight

This is worth remembering:

> **Model width is expensive because many learned matrices have dimensions involving dmodel2d_{model}^2.**

That's why changing:

512→1024512\rightarrow1024

is not a small change.

It affects:

- attention projections
    
- FFN projections
    
- embeddings/output-related components
    
- representation size
    
- computational cost
    
- memory requirements
    

This is one reason modern architecture design is fundamentally a problem of **capacity versus computation**.

---

# 21. Dropout

The original paper reports:

### Base

dropout=0.1dropout=0.1

### Big

dropout=0.3dropout=0.3

Dropout randomly removes activations during training with the specified probability.

For example:

```
Original:

[0.4, 0.8, 0.2, 0.6]

Dropout:

[0.4, 0,   0.2, 0]
```

Conceptually, it prevents the network from becoming overly dependent on particular activation pathways.

### Important distinction

Dropout is a **training-time regularization mechanism**.

It is not part of the mathematical definition of attention itself.

---

# 22. Why does Big use more dropout?

The paper reports the configuration, but we should be careful about attributing an unstated motivation.

### Original paper fact

The Big configuration uses:

0.30.3

dropout.

### What we should NOT say

> "The authors definitely increased dropout because Big overfits."

Unless the paper explicitly establishes that causal explanation, we shouldn't present it as the authors' stated reasoning.

### Reasonable modern interpretation

A larger model has greater representational capacity and may benefit from stronger regularization.

That's a plausible interpretation, but it is different from an explicit historical claim about the authors' motivation.

---

# 23. Base vs Big: architecture versus scale

This distinction is crucial.

```
                  SAME ARCHITECTURAL IDEA

        Encoder-Decoder Transformer
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          │                   │
        BASE                 BIG
          │                   │
     d_model=512         d_model=1024
     heads=8             heads=16
     d_ff=2048           d_ff=4096
     dropout=.1          dropout=.3
```

The conceptual architecture remains the same.

Big essentially gives the model more capacity.

---

# 24. Training configuration

The paper also reports different training configurations and computational resources for its experiments.

For example, the paper describes training the base model on **8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs**, with the reported training setup taking about **12 hours** for the base model. The Big model used considerably more computation and was trained on the same general GPU family with a larger computational budget.

The important lesson isn't simply memorizing the hardware.

It's understanding that:

> Architecture size and training budget are connected.

A larger model generally requires substantially more computation.

---

# 25. Reverse engineering

Now let's pretend someone gives you this:

```
Transformer(
    num_encoder_layers=6,
    num_decoder_layers=6,
    d_model=512,
    nhead=8,
    dim_feedforward=2048
)
```

Can you recognize the architecture?

Yes.

You can reconstruct:

```
N = 6

d_model = 512

h = 8

d_k ≈ 512 / 8
    = 64

d_v ≈ 512 / 8
    = 64

d_ff = 2048
```

That immediately tells you:

```
Encoder
  × 6

Decoder
  × 6

Each attention module
  8 heads

Each head
  64-dimensional Q/K/V

FFN
  512 → 2048 → 512
```

This is exactly the kind of **architecture-reading skill** we're trying to develop.

---

# 26. Code connection

A PyTorch-style configuration might look conceptually like:

```
d_model = 512
nhead = 8
num_encoder_layers = 6
num_decoder_layers = 6
dim_feedforward = 2048
dropout = 0.1
```

The important thing is that these aren't arbitrary Python numbers.

They encode the mathematical architecture:

```
d_model=512
      ↓
representation dimension

nhead=8
      ↓
8 attention heads

512 / 8 = 64
      ↓
head dimension

dim_feedforward=2048
      ↓
FFN:
512 → 2048 → 512

num_encoder_layers=6
      ↓
6 encoder blocks

num_decoder_layers=6
      ↓
6 decoder blocks
```

This is exactly how you should read Transformer code:

> **Don't read configuration values as isolated numbers. Translate each one into an architectural consequence.**

---

# 27. A subtle point about dkd_k

There is an important distinction between:

dmodeld_{model}

and:

dkd_k

They are **not the same concept**.

Base:

dmodel=512d_{model}=512

but each head:

dk=64d_k=64

Therefore:

dk=dmodelhd_k=\frac{d_{model}}{h}

for the original configurations.

For Base:

5128=64\frac{512}{8}=64

For Big:

102416=64\frac{1024}{16}=64

This means increasing dmodeld_{model} was accompanied by increasing the number of heads so that the per-head dimension remained 64.

---

# 28. Why this matters for scaled dot-product attention

Our attention equation is:

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)VAttention(Q,K,V) = softmax \left( \frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V

If:

dk=64d_k=64

then:

dk=64=8\sqrt{d_k}=\sqrt{64}=8

So every head in these original configurations performs:

QKT8\frac{QK^T}{8}

before softmax.

That's a beautiful connection between today's lesson and the earlier attention lessons.

The hyperparameter table isn't just a list of model sizes.

It determines the actual numbers appearing inside the attention computation.

---

# 29. One complete Base example

Suppose:

B=1,T=4B=1,\quad T=4

Base model:

dmodel=512d_{model}=512

Therefore:

```
Token IDs
[1,4]

Embedding
[1,4,512]

Q/K/V before head split
[1,4,512]

After splitting heads
[1,8,4,64]

QKᵀ
[1,8,4,4]

Softmax
[1,8,4,4]

Attention × V
[1,8,4,64]

Concatenate
[1,4,512]

Output projection
[1,4,512]
```

Then the residual connection operates on:

```
[1,4,512]
```

because the sublayer output must match the residual input.

This is one reason the architecture keeps returning to dmodeld_{model}.

---

# 30. What if we removed the six-layer stacking?

Suppose we used only:

N=1N=1

instead of:

N=6N=6

The architecture still works mathematically.

But the model has fewer sequential transformations.

```
N=1

Input
 ↓
Attention
 ↓
FFN
 ↓
Output
```

versus:

```
N=6

Input
 ↓
Attention + FFN
 ↓
Attention + FFN
 ↓
Attention + FFN
 ↓
Attention + FFN
 ↓
Attention + FFN
 ↓
Attention + FFN
 ↓
Output
```

The paper's experiments include ablations involving model depth, which we'll study separately because **that is experimental evidence**, rather than merely architectural intuition.

---

# 31. Common mistakes

### Mistake 1

Thinking:

> Base = 6 layers.

Not quite.

It is:

6 encoder+6 decoder6\text{ encoder}+6\text{ decoder}

### Mistake 2

Thinking:

> dmodel=dkd_{model}=d_k

No.

Base:

512≠64512\neq64

### Mistake 3

Thinking:

> Big has 16 dimensions per head.

No.

Big has:

16 heads×64 dimensions/head16\text{ heads}\times64\text{ dimensions/head}

### Mistake 4

Thinking:

> dffd_{ff} is the final representation dimension.

No.

It is the **inner dimension of the feed-forward network**.

### Mistake 5

Thinking:

> Big is a completely different Transformer.

No.

It is the same basic architecture with substantially larger dimensions and a different dropout setting.

If:

B=3,T=12B=3,T=12

and Base uses eight heads, what is the shape of the split Q tensor?

**Q7.**

What is the attention-score shape?

### Reverse engineering

**Q8.**

You see:

```
d_model = 1024
num_heads = 16
d_ff = 4096
```

Which original Transformer configuration does this strongly resemble?

### Implementation

**Q9.**

Why can't you simply reshape a `[B,T,512]` tensor into eight heads if the dimensions don't divide evenly?

---

# 34. What we learned

The most important lesson isn't the table itself.

It's this:

Configuration numbers describe the computational structure.\boxed{ \text{Configuration numbers describe the computational structure.} }

For the original Base Transformer:

dmodel=512,h=8,dk=dv=64,dff=2048,N=6\boxed{ d_{model}=512,\quad h=8,\quad d_k=d_v=64,\quad d_{ff}=2048,\quad N=6 }

For Big:

dmodel=1024,h=16,dk=dv=64,dff=4096,N=6\boxed{ d_{model}=1024,\quad h=16,\quad d_k=d_v=64,\quad d_{ff}=4096,\quad N=6 }

And therefore:

```
BASE

512-dimensional representation
        ↓
8 × 64-dimensional heads
        ↓
attention
        ↓
512-dimensional representation
        ↓
512 → 2048 → 512 FFN


BIG

1024-dimensional representation
        ↓
16 × 64-dimensional heads
        ↓
attention
        ↓
1024-dimensional representation
        ↓
1024 → 4096 → 1024 FFN
```

The deeper research skill is being able to see a configuration and mentally reconstruct the architecture.

---

# 35. Dependency graph update

We've now connected:

```
Multi-Head Attention
        ↓
d_model
        ↓
number of heads
        ↓
d_k / d_v
        ↓
attention tensor shapes
        ↓
FFN
        ↓
d_ff
        ↓
parameter count
        ↓
Base vs Big
```

So when you see:

512, 8, 64, 2048512,\ 8,\ 64,\ 2048

you should no longer see four arbitrary numbers.

You should see:

```
512-dimensional model
        ↓
8 attention heads
        ↓
64 dimensions/head
        ↓
512 → 2048 → 512 FFN
```

That's the reverse-engineering mindset we're building.

## Next: Lesson 35 — Complexity Analysis

We'll derive why the paper compares:

$$O(n2d)O(n^2d)$$

for self-attention against recurrent and convolutional approaches, and—more importantly—understand **why the Transformer trades quadratic sequence-length computation for dramatically better parallelization and shorter communication paths**.

# Lesson 35 — Complexity Analysis: original paper itself already recognized the long-sequence cost and mentioned restricted self-attention as a possible approach for future investigation sequence length changes from 1,000 to 2,000, by what factor does the number of entries in computation highly parallelizable and creates direct communication paths between positions, but the all-to-all matrix introduces quadratic scaling with sequence length Why Attention Was a Big Deal

Today we reach one of the **most important arguments in the original paper**.

The Transformer wasn't proposed merely because attention was fashionable. The authors made a specific architectural argument:

> If we replace recurrence with self-attention, we can make token-to-token communication much more direct and computation much more parallelizable, at the cost of quadratic dependence on sequence length.

That tradeoff is the heart of this lesson.

**Source of truth:** Vaswani et al., _Attention Is All You Need_, especially Section 4 and Table 1. DOI+1

---

# 1. Learning objective

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

without merely memorizing it.

You should understand:

- what O(n)O(n) means
    
- what O(n2)O(n^2) means
    
- why self-attention is quadratic in sequence length
    
- why RNNs are O(nd2)O(nd^2) in the paper's comparison
    
- why recurrence requires O(n)O(n) sequential operations
    
- why self-attention requires O(1)O(1) sequential operations
    
- what "maximum path length" means
    
- why shorter paths help long-range dependencies
    
- why the Transformer can be more parallelizable even when it performs a lot of computation
    
- why the quadratic attention cost eventually becomes a problem for very long sequences
    
- what the original paper actually claimed versus what later Transformer research discovered
    

---

# 2. Prerequisites

You already know:

QKTQK^T

and:

Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKTdk)VAttention(Q,K,V) = softmax\left( \frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V

You also know that if a sequence has nn tokens, then the attention-score matrix has shape:

[n,n][n,n]

That single fact is going to explain most of:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

---

# 3. First: What does O(⋅)O(\cdot) mean?

Let's start at Class-10 level.

Suppose you have 10 students.

You want every student to shake hands with every other student.

How many interactions are there?

Roughly:

10×10=10010\times10=100

Now suppose there are 100 students:

100×100=10,000100\times100=10,000

The number of possible pairwise interactions grows approximately with the **square** of the number of students.

That's:

O(n2)O(n^2)

where nn is the number of students.

---

# 4. What does O(n)O(n) mean?

Suppose instead that each student only needs to interact with the next student:

```
1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → ... → n
```

Then the number of interactions grows roughly proportionally to the number of students.

For 10:

O(10)O(10)

For 100:

O(100)O(100)

For 1,000:

O(1000)O(1000)

That's:

O(n)O(n)

---

# 5. The key difference

Imagine sequence length increasing:

|nn|nn|n2n^2|
|---|---|---|
|10|10|100|
|100|100|10,000|
|1,000|1,000|1,000,000|
|10,000|10,000|100,000,000|

This is why people often say:

> "Attention has a quadratic sequence-length cost."

Because if you double nn:

n→2nn\rightarrow2n

then:

n2→4n2n^2\rightarrow4n^2

So doubling sequence length can roughly quadruple the pairwise-attention work.

---

# 6. Now connect this to self-attention

Suppose:

```
The cat sat on the mat
```

There are:

n=6n=6

tokens.

Self-attention computes relationships between positions.

Conceptually:

```
             The cat sat on the mat
              ↕   ↕   ↕   ↕   ↕   ↕
The           ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓
cat           ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓
sat           ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓
on            ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓
the           ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓
mat           ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓   ✓
```

That produces an attention-score matrix:

[6,6][6,6]

More generally:

[n,n][n,n]

There are therefore:

n2n^2

pairwise scores.

That is the first major reason self-attention has a quadratic dependence on sequence length.

---

# 7. But why O(n2d)O(n^2d), not just O(n2)O(n^2)?

Excellent question.

Each attention score involves vectors with dimensionality dd.

For example:

qi⋅kjq_i\cdot k_j

Suppose:

qi,kj∈Rdq_i,k_j\in\mathbb R^d

Then their dot product requires roughly dd multiplications/additions.

There are approximately:

n2n^2

such interactions.

Therefore:

n2×dn^2\times d

gives:

O(n2d)\boxed{O(n^2d)}

This is the paper's self-attention complexity. NeurIPS Papers

---

# 8. Deriving it from matrix multiplication

Let's make this precise.

Suppose:

Q∈Rn×dQ\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}

and:

K∈Rn×dK\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}

Then:

KT∈Rd×nK^T\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}

Therefore:

QKTQK^T

has shape:

[n,d][d,n]=[n,n][n,d][d,n] = [n,n]

Matrix multiplication of:

[n,d][n,d]

by:

[d,n][d,n]

requires approximately:

n×n×dn\times n\times d

multiplications.

Therefore:

O(n2d)\boxed{O(n^2d)}

---

# 9. This is the mathematical origin of quadratic attention

Remember:

QKTQK^T

isn't merely a mysterious equation.

It is literally asking:

> For every query position, how well does it match every key position?

There are:

nn

queries.

Each compares against:

nn

keys.

Therefore:

n×n=n2n\times n=n^2

comparisons.

Each comparison operates over dd dimensions.

Therefore:

n2d\boxed{n^2d}

---

# 10. What about AVAV?

After computing:

A=softmax(QKTdk)A= softmax\left( \frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)

we have:

A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}

and:

V∈Rn×dV\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}

Then:

AVAV

has shape:

[n,n][n,d]=[n,d][n,n][n,d] = [n,d]

Its computational cost is also approximately:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

So the core attention operation has the characteristic quadratic sequence-length dependence.

---

# 11. Tensor-shape view

Let's use:

B=2B=2

T=n=100T=n=100

dmodel=512d_{model}=512

and temporarily ignore heads.

We have:

Q:[2,100,512]Q:[2,100,512]

K:[2,100,512]K:[2,100,512]

Then:

QKT:[2,100,100]QK^T:[2,100,100]

Notice the important part:

100×100100\times100

That is the pairwise token-interaction matrix.

If we increase:

T=100→1000T=100\rightarrow1000

then the attention matrix changes from:

100×100100\times100

to:

1000×10001000\times1000

which means:

10,000→1,000,00010,000\rightarrow1,000,000

attention entries per head and batch element.

That's a 100× increase in the number of attention entries even though sequence length only increased 10×.

---

# 12. Now compare RNNs

The original paper compares self-attention against recurrent layers.

Its Table 1 gives:

O(n2d)\boxed{O(n^2d)}

for self-attention and:

O(nd2)\boxed{O(nd^2)}

for recurrent layers. NeurIPS Papers

Why?

Let's reconstruct it.

---

# 13. RNN computation

Consider a simple RNN:

ht=f(Whht−1+Wxxt)h_t=f(W_hh_{t-1}+W_xx_t)

Suppose the hidden representation has dimension:

dd

Then WhW_h is approximately:

[d,d][d,d]

Matrix multiplication:

Whht−1W_hh_{t-1}

costs approximately:

d2d^2

operations.

And there are:

nn

time steps.

Therefore:

n×d2n\times d^2

giving:

O(nd2)\boxed{O(nd^2)}

This is the paper's simplified recurrent-layer complexity comparison.

---

# 14. But there's something even more important than arithmetic

Imagine:

```
x1 → h1
      ↓
x2 → h2
      ↓
x3 → h3
      ↓
x4 → h4
      ↓
x5 → h5
```

You cannot compute:

h5h_5

until:

h4h_4

exists.

You cannot compute:

h4h_4

until:

h3h_3

exists.

And so on.

Therefore:

h1→h2→h3→⋯→hnh_1\rightarrow h_2\rightarrow h_3\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow h_n

creates a chain of dependencies.

---

# 15. Sequential operations

The original paper calls this:

O(n)O(n)

sequential operations.

This is one of the most important numbers in Table 1.

For an RNN:

```
Step 1
 ↓
Step 2
 ↓
Step 3
 ↓
...
 ↓
Step n
```

You have roughly nn sequential steps.

The next step depends on the previous one.

---

# 16. Self-attention is different

For self-attention:

```
x1 ─────┐
x2 ─────┤
x3 ─────┼──→ Q, K, V → attention
x4 ─────┤
x5 ─────┘
```

The Q/K/V projections for all positions can be computed using matrix operations.

Then the attention matrix can be computed as a large matrix multiplication.

Modern hardware such as GPUs is particularly good at these large parallel matrix operations.

So the paper characterizes self-attention as requiring:

O(1)\boxed{O(1)}

sequential operations per layer. NeurIPS Papers

---

# 17. Important clarification: O(1)O(1) does NOT mean "free"

This is a common misunderstanding.

When the paper says self-attention has:

O(1)O(1)

sequential operations, it does **not** mean:

> "The entire attention calculation requires one tiny operation."

It means:

> The number of dependency-ordered sequential stages does not grow with sequence length in the same way as recurrence.

There can still be **a huge amount of parallel computation**.

Think:

```
RNN:

Token 1
  ↓
Token 2
  ↓
Token 3
  ↓
Token 4
```

versus:

```
Self-attention:

Token 1 ─┐
Token 2 ─┤
Token 3 ─┼──→ large parallel computation
Token 4 ─┤
```

---

# 18. Why GPUs love the second structure

Suppose you need to calculate:

q1k1, q1k2, q1k3,…q_1k_1,\ q_1k_2,\ q_1k_3,\ldots

and similarly for all other queries.

These operations can be represented as matrix multiplication.

GPUs are designed to execute many numerical operations simultaneously.

So self-attention converts much of the sequence computation into large dense matrix operations.

This is one of the major practical reasons the Transformer could exploit hardware parallelism effectively.

The original paper explicitly emphasized improved parallelizability and reduced training time. arXiv

---

# 19. Now we reach "maximum path length"

This phrase sounds complicated.

It isn't.

Imagine information from:

```
"The"
```

needs to influence:

```
"mat"
```

How many computational steps does information have to travel through?

That's the intuition behind **path length**.

---

# 20. RNN path length

Consider:

```
The → cat → sat → on → the → mat
```

In a recurrent model, information from the first token may have to pass through:

```
h1
 ↓
h2
 ↓
h3
 ↓
h4
 ↓
h5
 ↓
h6
```

So the path grows with:

nn

The paper therefore gives recurrent networks:

O(n)\boxed{O(n)}

maximum path length. NeurIPS Papers

---

# 21. Self-attention path length

Now consider self-attention.

Every token can directly attend to every other token.

Therefore:

```
"The" ─────────────────→ "mat"
```

can happen within the same attention layer.

The maximum path length is therefore:

O(1)\boxed{O(1)}

The paper's Table 1 gives exactly this comparison. NeurIPS Papers

---

# 22. Why does shorter path length matter?

The authors explicitly motivate this by saying that learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in sequence transduction, and that shorter paths make it easier for information and gradients to travel between distant positions. OakTrust

Imagine trying to send a message:

### Architecture A

```
A → B → C → D → E → F → G
```

versus:

### Architecture B

```
A ─────────────→ G
```

The second architecture provides a direct computational connection.

That doesn't automatically guarantee better learning in every circumstance, but it changes the information-flow structure dramatically.

---

# 23. Three different things you must not confuse

This lesson contains three separate concepts:

### 1. Computational complexity

How much arithmetic is required?

For self-attention:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

### 2. Sequential operations

How many computation stages must happen one after another?

Self-attention:

O(1)O(1)

Recurrent:

O(n)O(n)

### 3. Maximum path length

How many layers/steps can separate two positions?

Self-attention:

O(1)O(1)

Recurrent:

O(n)O(n)

These are related, but they are **not the same quantity**.

---

# 24. The original paper's Table 1

Here is the central comparison from the paper:

|Layer type|Complexity per layer|Sequential operations|Maximum path length|
|---|---|---|---|
|Self-attention|O(n2d)O(n^2d)|O(1)O(1)|O(1)O(1)|
|Recurrent|O(nd2)O(nd^2)|O(n)O(n)|O(n)O(n)|
|Convolutional|O(knd2)O(knd^2)|O(1)O(1)|O(log⁡kn)O(\log_k n)|
|Restricted self-attention|O(rnd)O(rnd)|O(1)O(1)|O(n/r)O(n/r)|

This is directly from the original paper's complexity table. NeurIPS Papers

Now let's understand every row rather than memorize it.

---

# 25. Convolutional sequence models

The paper also considers convolution.

Suppose a convolution has kernel width:

kk

and sequence length:

nn

The paper gives:

O(knd2)\boxed{O(knd^2)}

per layer. NeurIPS Papers

Why isn't the path length immediately O(1)O(1)?

Because a convolution with a small kernel doesn't necessarily connect distant positions directly.

For example, with:

k=3k=3

you might have:

```
x1 x2 x3
   x2 x3 x4
      x3 x4 x5
```

A token can see nearby positions.

But for:

```
x1 → x100
```

you need multiple layers for information to travel across the sequence.

---

# 26. Why O(log⁡kn)O(\log_k n) for certain convolutions?

The paper notes that with **dilated convolutions**, the maximum path length can become:

O(log⁡kn)O(\log_k n)

rather than O(n)O(n). NeurIPS Papers

The intuition is that each layer can expand the receptive field substantially.

For example:

```
Layer 1:
• •
```

then:

```
Layer 2:
•   •
```

then:

```
Layer 3:
•       •
```

The receptive field can grow rapidly.

So convolution is more parallelizable than recurrence, but direct all-to-all communication is still a special advantage of self-attention.

---

# 27. Restricted self-attention

Here's an important subtlety.

The authors themselves recognized that:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

could become expensive for very long sequences.

They proposed the idea of restricting attention to a neighborhood of size:

rr

Then complexity becomes:

O(rnd)\boxed{O(rnd)}

instead of:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

according to Table 1. OakTrust

But there's a tradeoff.

Maximum path length becomes:

O(n/r)\boxed{O(n/r)}

instead of:

O(1)O(1)

---

# 28. This is an extremely important insight

The paper is already describing a tradeoff that later Transformer research would revisit extensively:

```
Full attention

More direct communication
        ↓
O(n²d)
```

versus:

```
Restricted attention

Less computation
        ↓
O(rnd)

but

longer communication paths
```

This is why later work on efficient attention, sparse attention, local attention, and related techniques exists.

### Important historical distinction

Those later techniques are **not part of the original 2017 Transformer architecture**.

We're mentioning them only to understand the significance of the tradeoff the original paper identified.

---

# 29. The condition n<dn<d

The paper makes an interesting observation:

Self-attention's:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

is less than recurrent:

O(nd2)O(nd^2)

when:

n<dn<d

Let's derive that.

We want:

n2d<nd2n^2d < nd^2

Divide by ndnd:

n<dn<d

That's it.

So if:

n<dn<d

self-attention has lower asymptotic arithmetic complexity under this simplified comparison.

The paper notes that this was often the case for sentence representations in machine translation at the time, including word-piece and byte-pair representations. OakTrust

---

# 30. Numerical example

Suppose:

n=100n=100

and:

d=512d=512

### Self-attention

n2dn^2d

=1002×512=100^2\times512

=10,000×512=10,000\times512

=5,120,000=5,120,000

roughly:

5.1M5.1M

units of the asymptotic operation count.

### Recurrent

nd2nd^2

=100×5122=100\times512^2

=100×262,144=100\times262,144

=26,214,400=26,214,400

roughly:

26.2M26.2M

So under this simplified comparison, self-attention requires substantially fewer arithmetic operations.

---

# 31. But now make the sequence very long

Suppose:

n=5000n=5000

and:

d=512d=512

Self-attention:

50002×5125000^2\times512

=25,000,000×512=25,000,000\times512

=12,800,000,000=12,800,000,000

That is approximately:

12.8 billion12.8\text{ billion}

in this simplified n2dn^2d scaling.

Meanwhile recurrence:

5000×51225000\times512^2

=1,310,720,000=1,310,720,000

approximately:

1.31 billion1.31\text{ billion}

So now the quadratic sequence-length cost becomes significant.

This is why:

> **"Transformers are parallel" does not mean "Transformers are computationally cheap."**

---

# 32. This distinction is essential

Self-attention provides:

### Advantage

O(1)O(1)

sequential dependency depth per layer.

### Cost

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

arithmetic scaling with sequence length.

So the Transformer essentially makes this trade:

```
                 TRANSFORMER TRADEOFF

        Remove recurrence
               ↓
       better parallelism
               ↓
     shorter dependency paths
               ↓
      direct token interaction
               │
               ↓
       BUT attention matrix
               ↓
          n × n
               ↓
         quadratic cost
```

That tradeoff is one of the central ideas you should remember.

---

# 33. Tensor-shape interpretation

Let's make the quadratic cost visually obvious.

Suppose:

T=4T=4

Then:

Q:[4,d]Q:[4,d]

K:[4,d]K:[4,d]

and:

QKT:[4,4]QK^T:[4,4]

The matrix is:

```
          Keys
        1  2  3  4
      ┌─────────────
Q  1 │ •  •  •  •
u  2 │ •  •  •  •
e  3 │ •  •  •  •
r  4 │ •  •  •  •
s    └─────────────
```

There are:

42=164^2=16

scores.

Now:

T=100T=100

means:

1002=10,000100^2=10,000

scores.

And:

T=10,000T=10,000

means:

100,000,000100,000,000

scores.

That's the quadratic wall.

---

# 34. What about multiple heads?

Good question.

For multi-head attention:

hh

heads each have a score matrix roughly:

[T,T][T,T]

So you can conceptually have:

```
Head 1 → [T,T]
Head 2 → [T,T]
...
Head h → [T,T]
```

The total attention representation is arranged so that the model dimension remains:

dmodeld_{model}

For the original Base model:

h=8h=8

and:

dk=dv=64d_k=d_v=64

so:

8×64=5128\times64=512

The complexity analysis in the paper is stated in terms of nn and dd, rather than requiring you to separately memorize a different asymptotic formula for every head.

---

# 35. Training versus inference: important distinction

There's another subtle point.

The original complexity discussion concerns **layers and sequence processing**, especially training/parallel computation.

But during autoregressive decoding, the decoder generates:

```
token 1
   ↓
token 2
   ↓
token 3
   ↓
token 4
```

one token at a time.

So:

> The Transformer removes recurrence from the architecture, but autoregressive generation itself remains sequential.

This distinction becomes very important when you later study modern decoder-only language models.

For today's lesson, don't confuse:

**parallel training computation**

with:

**sequential autoregressive generation**.

---

# 36. Reverse engineering exercise

Imagine someone gives you this architecture:

```
Input
 ↓
QKV projections
 ↓
T × T attention matrix
 ↓
weighted values
 ↓
FFN
```

and tells you:

T=2048T=2048

Ask yourself:

> What object is potentially becoming very large?

Answer:

T×TT\times T

So:

204822048^2

=4,194,304=4,194,304

attention entries **per head** for one sequence.

That's already over four million entries.

Now increase:

2048→40962048\rightarrow4096

Then:

40962=16,777,2164096^2 = 16,777,216

The sequence doubled.

The attention matrix became **four times larger**.

That is quadratic scaling.

---

# 37. Common mistakes

## Mistake 1: "Quadratic means the whole Transformer is O(n2)O(n^2)."

Not exactly.

The paper's statement is about the **self-attention layer's per-layer complexity**:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

There are other computations too.

---

## Mistake 2: "O(1) sequential operations means constant total computation."

No.

It means the number of dependency-ordered sequential stages doesn't grow with nn in the same way.

The total arithmetic can still grow as:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

---

## Mistake 3: "RNNs are bad because they have O(nd2)O(nd^2)."

That's too simplistic.

The original paper's argument considers multiple factors:

- computational complexity
    
- sequential operations
    
- maximum path length
    
- parallelization
    

It's the **combination** that matters.

---

## Mistake 4: "Attention is always cheaper than RNNs."

No.

The paper specifically notes the self-attention arithmetic advantage under the condition:

n<dn<d

And for very long sequences, quadratic scaling becomes expensive.

---

## Mistake 5: "The Transformer solved long-context computation permanently."

No.

The original paper solved one important bottleneck—sequential recurrence—but introduced another scaling challenge:

O(n2)O(n^2)

attention interactions.

Later research has explored many ways of addressing this.

Those later methods should not be retroactively inserted into the 2017 architecture.

---

# 38. Research-paper reading skill

Here's how to read this section of the paper scientifically.

### Author claim

The paper argues that self-attention has:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

per-layer complexity, O(1)O(1) sequential operations, and O(1)O(1) maximum path length. NeurIPS Papers

### Experimental evidence

The paper reports strong translation performance and substantially reduced training time relative to systems cited in the paper. arXiv

### Interpretation

One reasonable interpretation is that the architecture's parallelizable structure helped exploit modern hardware effectively.

### Your inference

You might conclude:

> "Direct token-to-token connections are likely useful for learning long-range relationships."

That's reasonable, but you should distinguish your inference from the literal experimental evidence.

This distinction is essential when reading research papers.

---

# 39. Original paper vs later development

### Original 2017 Transformer

Uses full self-attention with:

O(n2d)O(n^2d)

sequence-length scaling.

### Later research

Many later methods attempt to reduce the cost of long-context attention.

Examples include:

- local/sliding-window attention
    
- sparse attention
    
- approximate attention
    
- memory-efficient implementations
    
- FlashAttention
    
- various long-context architectures
    

But these are **later developments**.

They should not be described as components of the original 2017 Transformer.

The original paper itself already recognized the long-sequence cost and mentioned restricted self-attention as a possible approach for future investigation. OakTrust

---

# 40. The deeper lesson

Let's return to the central chain you've been building.

We started with:

```
RNN
 ↓
Sequential dependency
 ↓
Hard to parallelize
 ↓
Long path between distant tokens
```

The Transformer says:

```
Replace recurrence
       ↓
Self-attention
       ↓
Every position can communicate directly
       ↓
Parallel matrix operations
       ↓
Short path length
```

But the price is:

```
Every position
     ↕
Every other position
     ↓
T × T attention matrix
     ↓
O(n²d)
```

That is the fundamental tradeoff.

---

# 41. One equation to remember

If you remember only one derivation from this lesson, remember:

Q∈Rn×dQ\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}

KT∈Rd×nK^T\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}

therefore:

QKT∈Rn×nQK^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}

and matrix multiplication costs approximately:

n×n×dn\times n\times d

so:

O(n2d)\boxed{O(n^2d)}

The complexity isn't arbitrary.

**It falls directly out of the shape of the attention matrix.**

---

# 42. Dependency graph update

Our graph now becomes:

```
Vectors
   ↓
Matrices
   ↓
Matrix multiplication
   ↓
Q, K, V
   ↓
QKᵀ
   ↓
[n × n] attention matrix
   ↓
O(n²d)
   ↓
Parallel self-attention
   ↓
O(1) sequential operations
   ↓
O(1) path length
   ↓
Transformer's computational tradeoff
```

And the competing path is:

```
RNN
 ↓
hₜ depends on hₜ₋₁
 ↓
O(n) sequential operations
 ↓
O(n) path length
 ↓
O(nd²) recurrent-layer complexity
```

# 45. Summary

The original Transformer made a fundamental architectural tradeoff.

### RNN

O(nd2)\boxed{O(nd^2)}

O(n) sequential operations\boxed{O(n)\text{ sequential operations}}

O(n) maximum path length\boxed{O(n)\text{ maximum path length}}

### Self-attention

O(n2d)\boxed{O(n^2d)}

O(1) sequential operations\boxed{O(1)\text{ sequential operations}}

O(1) maximum path length\boxed{O(1)\text{ maximum path length}}

The key insight is:

> **Self-attention replaces a long sequential chain with an all-to-all interaction matrix.**

That makes computation highly parallelizable and creates direct communication paths between positions, but the all-to-all matrix introduces quadratic scaling with sequence length. This is exactly the tradeoff highlighted in the original paper. NeurIPS Papers

---

# 46. What we learned

You should now be able to look at:

QKTQK^T

and see **three things simultaneously**:

### Intuition

> Every token compares itself with every other token.

### Mathematics

[n,d][d,n]=[n,n][n,d][d,n]=[n,n]

### Complexity

n2 pairwise interactions×d=O(n2d)n^2\text{ pairwise interactions}\times d = O(n^2d)

That is the kind of thinking we want to build throughout this course.
